transcript.question: Now I'd like to talk about a specific situation. When you or your team needs to recruit new talent, how do you typically handle that today? What software or tools do you use?

Beyond that, we use LinkedIn Recruiter for sourcing, which is basically table stakes at this point. We also use Gem for outbound sequencing and candidate relationship management, which I love because it lets us track response rates and optimize our messaging. For scheduling we use Modernloop, which automates a lot of the back-and-forth of coordinating panel interviews. Oh, and we use Metaview for interview transcription and note-taking, which has been a game changer for training junior interviewers. And then we have Hired for some engineering roles where we want candidates to come to us. So it's, yeah, quite a stack when you list it all out.

transcript.question: Thanks. When you try to recruit new talent, what does a really good outcome look like for you? Why is this important to you or your team?
transcript.response: Oh, that's a really good question. So for me, a great outcome is multidimensional. First, the candidate has to be genuinely excited about the role, not just accepting because it's their best offer. I've seen too many hires where someone joins for the comp and then they're disengaged within six months. Second, they need to meet our technical or functional bar, obviously. Third, and this is something I care a lot about personally, we want every hiring process to result in a candidate who would refer us to a friend regardless of whether they got the offer or not. That's the candidate experience piece. We actually survey candidates post-process and track our NPS score, which right now is hovering around 72, which I'm pretty proud of. Why does it matter? Well, we're in a competitive market in San Francisco for engineering talent. Our reputation as an employer is everything. One bad Glassdoor review from a candidate who had a terrible interview experience can cost us downstream. And from a business perspective, every open role is lost productivity. Our CEO literally tracks open reqs as a drag on quarterly OKRs. So there's real pressure to fill roles quickly with the right people.

transcript.question: Got it. How would you describe your level of satisfaction with how you're currently recruiting new talent? What's working well and what's not?
transcript.response: I'd give us an eight out of ten, honestly. I'm pretty proud of what we've built. Every candidate goes through the same stages, gets evaluated on the same criteria, and our hiring managers trust the data they see in the scorecards. Gem has been fantastic for outbound, our response rates are in the low 30s which is well above industry average. Modernloop saves my team probably 10 hours a week in scheduling coordination. And the data is never perfectly clean because, you know, naming conventions differ between systems, date formats are different, some candidates exist in multiple systems under slightly different names. It's maddening. I'd say it's a seven out of ten frustration for me personally. For my team, the bigger frustration is actually hiring manager responsiveness. transcript.question: Lastly, looking at your business at a broader level, what would you say are the biggest challenges affecting your business that are also directly affecting your team?

transcript.response: So our recruiting is, I'd say, a mix of formal and informal channels. For our ATS, we use Lever, which we implemented about a year ago. Before that we were using, honestly, a pretty embarrassing combination of Google Sheets and our CRM, Salesforce, to track candidates. The Lever implementation was a big improvement. Beyond Lever, we use LinkedIn heavily, both LinkedIn Recruiter for proactive sourcing and regular LinkedIn jobs for postings. For financial advisor roles specifically, we work with a couple of specialized executive search firms because those roles are extremely hard to fill. People who manage $50 million client portfolios don't typically respond to job postings, right? They need to be recruited personally through trusted relationships. For our operations and corporate roles, we rely more on Indeed and referrals. Our employee referral program is pretty strong, we pay $5,000 for advisor referrals and $2,500 for other roles. transcript.question: Thanks. When you try to recruit new talent, what does a really good outcome look like for you? Why is this important to you or your team?
transcript.response: This really depends on the role, so let me break it down. For financial advisors, which are our highest-impact hires, a great outcome is bringing on someone with an existing book of business who integrates well with our client-first culture. Those hires typically take six months to fully onboard because of the regulatory requirements and the complexity of transitioning client relationships. A great advisor hire can add $10 million or more in assets under management in their first year, so the business impact is massive. For client service roles, a good outcome is someone who's detail-oriented, empathetic, and can handle the sometimes stressful dynamic of working with high-net-worth clients who are, shall we say, demanding. We want those folks to stay at least three years. For operations and tech roles, we're looking for people who can bring modern practices to what is, honestly, a pretty traditional industry. A lot of wealth management firms are still running on legacy systems, and we're trying to be more progressive. So we need people who can drive change without alienating our more traditional colleagues. Why is all of this important? Because in wealth management, client trust is everything. Our clients are trusting us with their life savings and their family's financial future. The quality of every single employee, from the advisor to the person answering the phone, directly impacts that trust. One bad hire in a client-facing role can literally cost us a $100 million relationship.

transcript.question: Got it. How would you describe your level of satisfaction with how you're currently recruiting new talent? What's working well and what's not?
transcript.response: I'd say about a six. What's working well, Lever has been a big upgrade for us in terms of process organization. We can actually see our pipeline now, which sounds basic but it was a huge step forward from spreadsheets. Our referral program works really well, probably 35% of our hires come through referrals. And the executive search firms do a good job for advisor recruitment, they earn their fees. What's not working, the cost of recruiting financial advisors is astronomical. transcript.question: With your current approach, what causes the biggest frustration? Please describe it and the level of frustration it causes you or your team.

We don't have the relationships or the sourcing capability to find senior advisors on our own, so we keep paying search firms, which means less budget for building internal capability, which means we keep paying search firms. It's a catch-22. I'd rate that frustration a nine out of ten because it's a strategic problem, not just an operational annoyance. The other frustration, and this is more of a tools thing, is that our three offices operate somewhat independently when it comes to recruiting. We don't have great visibility across offices into who's hiring whom, and sometimes two offices will be reaching out to the same candidate without knowing it. That's happened at least twice this year and it's embarrassing. That's probably a six out of ten.

transcript.question: Now, I'd like you to think back to the last time your team considered buying a new recruiting tool. How long ago was that?
transcript.response: That was about 14 months ago when we chose Lever. Before that we'd never had a proper ATS so it was our first real purchase in this category. We knew we needed to professionalize our recruiting as the firm grew.

transcript.question: What recruiting tool were you using at the time and which recruiting tools did you consider buying?
transcript.response: We were using Google Sheets and Salesforce, basically cobbling together a workflow from tools that weren't designed for recruiting. We evaluated Lever, BambooHR, and Greenhouse.

transcript.question: Was a contract for your existing tool expiring? And were you happy or frustrated with your existing tool?
transcript.response: No contract since we didn't have a recruiting tool. We were frustrated with the manual process. transcript.question: Were there any changes in your business that motivated your team to consider buying a new recruiting tool? Did your recruiting needs change?
transcript.response: Yes, a couple of things converged. Second, our CEO committed to growing the firm to $20 billion in AUM over the next five years, which meant a significant hiring ramp. And third, we had a compliance scare where we couldn't produce proper documentation for a hiring decision that was questioned. That was the final push. The CEO basically said, we need a real system, make it happen.

transcript.question: Which recruiting tools did you consider? Please list the names of the tools you considered.
transcript.response: Lever, BambooHR, and Greenhouse.

transcript.question: After looking at those tools, did you purchase one or just continue using your current tool?
transcript.response: We purchased Lever.

transcript.question: If you purchased one, which one did you purchase and what attracted you to it? How did it stand out from the others you considered?
transcript.response: We chose Lever primarily for the CRM functionality. In wealth management, advisor recruitment is all about relationships. transcript.question: For each of the tools that you considered, but decided not to purchase, please share the main reasons why each tool was not chosen.

No CRM capability, limited pipeline analytics, and the compliance documentation features weren't robust enough for a regulated financial services firm. It would have been fine for a company without our specific needs. Greenhouse was honestly a really strong contender. The structured interviewing features are excellent and I loved their focus on reducing hiring bias. But two things knocked them out. First, the CRM wasn't as developed as Lever's, and that was our number one requirement. Second, the pricing was meaningfully higher, like 30% more than Lever, and for a 200-person firm in a pretty conservative industry, I had to be thoughtful about the cost conversation with our CFO. If CRM hadn't been our top priority, we probably would have gone with Greenhouse.

transcript.question: Got it. Now, I'd like to ask you about a few specific recruiting tools. To start, have you heard of BambooHR? If you have, how would you describe it to a colleague? And please share how you feel about this brand? Good or bad.
transcript.response: Yes, we evaluated them recently. I'd describe BambooHR as a really well-designed HR platform for small to mid-size businesses. transcript.question: Have you heard of Workday? If you have, how would you describe it to a colleague? And please share how you feel about this brand? Good or bad.
transcript.response: Of course, you can't be in HR without knowing Workday. I'd describe it as the 800-pound gorilla of enterprise HR and finance software. On one hand, it's clearly a powerful platform and the brand carries a lot of weight, like, saying you're on Workday signals that you're a serious company. On the other hand, I've heard from peers at larger firms that it's incredibly complex to implement and maintain, and you basically need a dedicated admin or even a small team just for Workday. For our size, it's completely out of scope. But I respect what they've built.

transcript.question: Lastly, have you heard of Greenhouse? If you have, how would you describe it to a colleague? And please share how you feel about this brand? Good or bad.
transcript.response: Yes, we evaluated Greenhouse and I was quite impressed. Their big differentiator is the structured interviewing philosophy, this idea that every candidate should be evaluated consistently using predefined criteria. That resonates with me philosophically. My feeling is very positive. The product is mature and thoughtful. We just couldn't justify the premium over Lever given that CRM was our top priority and Lever's CRM is stronger. But Greenhouse is an excellent product and I could see us reconsidering them down the road if our needs shift more toward structured hiring rigor.

transcript.question: Can you please confirm the main tool that your team uses to recruit new talent?
transcript.response: Lever.

transcript.question: On an annual basis, how much, roughly, do you think your company spends on that tool?
transcript.response: Lever costs us about $20,000 a year. When you add in LinkedIn Recruiter seats for two people, that's another $20,000 or so. transcript.question: Do you think the cost is reasonable relative to the value your company gets?
transcript.response: For Lever, absolutely. Twenty thousand dollars for a tool that gave us our first real recruiting process is a bargain. transcript.question: Now, please think back to the biggest frustration with your current tool that you shared earlier. Imagine that a feature could be added to your current solution that would solve that frustration. How much do you think that would be worth to your company on an annual basis?
transcript.response: So the biggest frustration is the search firm dependency. If Lever or a tool integrated with Lever could help us proactively identify and engage senior financial advisor candidates, essentially doing some of what our search firms do but at a fraction of the cost, that would be transformative. Even if we could bring just two or three advisor hires in-house instead of using a search firm, that's $150,000 to $300,000 in saved fees. So what would I pay for that feature? transcript.question: Lastly, looking at your business at a broader level, what would you say are the biggest challenges affecting your business that are also directly affecting your team?
transcript.response: The biggest challenge is the advisor retirement wave. The other challenge is technology modernization. Our clients increasingly expect digital experiences, online portals, mobile apps, real-time reporting, and we need to hire people who can build and maintain that technology. But those people want to work at tech companies, not wealth management firms. So we're competing for tech talent against Microsoft and Amazon and every startup in Seattle, and we can't match their comp or their brand appeal. We have to sell the stability, the mission, and the impact. It works sometimes, but it's an uphill battle.

Our work spans the traditional accounting services, audit, tax, and assurance, plus a growing advisory and consulting practice that does management consulting, technology advisory, forensic accounting, and risk management. It's a professional services firm through and through, so our business is literally our people. That phrase gets thrown around a lot in corporate speak but it's literally true for us because we don't sell a product, we sell the expertise and judgment of our professionals.

transcript.question: Now I'd like to talk about a specific situation. When you or your team needs to recruit new talent, how do you typically handle that today? What software or tools do you use?
transcript.response: Okay, so our recruiting operation is fairly complex because we have two very distinct hiring channels that operate almost independently. First is campus recruiting, which is massive for us and is really the lifeblood of the firm. We recruit at about 40 universities every year, primarily targeting accounting programs but increasingly also looking at data analytics, IT, and finance programs as our advisory practice grows. We use Handshake as our primary campus recruiting platform, and that's where we manage all of our on-campus events, information sessions, applications, and offers for entry-level positions. For experienced hires, which is our second channel, we use iCIMS as our main ATS. That handles all the lateral hire activity, requisitions, candidate tracking, interview management, offers, compliance documentation. We also use LinkedIn Recruiter extensively for sourcing experienced candidates, particularly in our advisory and consulting practice where the talent market is extremely competitive. We have a referral program running through iCIMS that generates solid results. And beyond the technology, we're very active at industry conferences, we have relationships with professional associations like the AICPA and state CPA societies, and we do a lot of networking-based recruiting that's very relationship-driven. The recruiting team is 12 people, split about evenly between campus and experienced hire.

transcript.question: Thanks. When you try to recruit new talent, what does a really good outcome look like for you? Why is this important to you or your team?
transcript.response: Oh, this is something I could talk about all day. So the answer is very different depending on which channel you're talking about. For campus recruiting, a great outcome is hiring a class of 150 to 200 entry-level accountants and consultants who pass the CPA exam within their first year, get strong performance reviews, and stay with the firm for at least three years. That three-year mark is important because that's roughly when they transition from being a net cost, where we're investing heavily in training and development, to being a net contributor, where they're billing clients independently and generating revenue. The CPA pass rate is also critical because we need licensed CPAs to sign off on audit work. If we hire 200 people and only 120 pass the CPA exam, we have a compliance problem and a staffing shortfall. For experienced hires, a great outcome is landing a senior manager or partner-track professional from a Big Four firm or a strong national competitor who brings client relationships, technical expertise, and the ability to develop junior staff. One excellent experienced hire at the senior manager or director level can bring in seven figures of revenue. Why does all of this matter at the highest level? Because professional services operates on a pyramid model. You need a steady flow of people entering at the bottom, progressing through the ranks, and eventually either making partner or transitioning out. And you need targeted experienced hires to fill gaps in the middle and top when internal progression can't keep up with growth. If the pipeline breaks at any level, the whole firm suffers.

transcript.question: Got it. How would you describe your level of satisfaction with how you're currently recruiting new talent? What's working well and what's not?
transcript.response: I'd say about a six out of ten, maybe a six and a half. The campus recruiting side is actually working pretty well, which is encouraging. Handshake is a solid platform and our on-campus presence is strong. We've built deep relationships with career services offices at our target schools over many years, and those relationships generate a steady flow of qualified candidates. We consistently fill our entry-level classes. The experienced hire side is where my satisfaction drops. iCIMS is adequate but not exceptional. The core tracking and compliance features work fine, and the reporting meets our regulatory requirements. But the sourcing tools within iCIMS are weak, which means we're heavily dependent on LinkedIn Recruiter, and that's expensive. The other big issue is our interview process for experienced hires, which is too long and too complicated. It can take four to six weeks from first conversation to offer letter, and that's too slow in a competitive market. On the positive side, our referral program is strong, generating about 35 percent of experienced hires. And iCIMS handles the compliance side well, which matters for SOC 2 reporting and the various regulatory requirements we operate under.

transcript.question: With your current approach, what causes the biggest frustration? Please describe it and the level of frustration it causes you or your team.
transcript.response: The interview process length for experienced hires is my biggest frustration, hands down, no question. Let me walk you through what happens and you'll understand why it drives me crazy. A candidate comes in for an initial phone screen with a recruiter. Then they do a video interview with the hiring manager. Then they need to interview with the practice leader for that service line. Then potentially a partner needs to meet them, especially for senior positions. And after all the interviews are done, we have a calibration meeting where the hiring manager, practice leader, and usually an HR partner discuss the candidate and reach consensus. Each of those steps has scheduling delays because these are busy professionals who bill by the hour and genuinely don't want to take time away from client work to interview candidates. I get it, their utilization rate is what the firm measures them on. But a process that could theoretically complete in two weeks ends up taking five or six because of scheduling gaps. And during that time, Big Four firms and other competitors are moving faster. They're extending offers while we're still trying to get a partner's calendar to open up. The frustration level is probably an eight or nine out of ten because I know we're losing excellent candidates to our own slowness. I've had candidates tell me directly, face to face, that they accepted another offer because we took too long. Hearing that after you've invested weeks of effort in building a relationship with that candidate is genuinely painful.

transcript.question: Which recruiting tools did you consider? Please list the names of the tools you considered.
transcript.response: Workday Recruiting, Greenhouse, and SAP SuccessFactors. All three got formal evaluations with multiple rounds of demos, reference calls with current customers, and detailed cost analysis.

transcript.question: After looking at those tools, did you purchase one or just continue using your current tool?
transcript.response: We renewed with iCIMS. After all that evaluation work, we ended up staying with our current platform.

transcript.question: If you purchased one, which one did you purchase and what attracted you to it? How did it stand out from the others you considered?
transcript.response: We didn't purchase a new tool. The evaluation was valuable because it gave us confidence that iCIMS, while not perfect, was still a reasonable choice for our needs. transcript.question: For each of the tools that you considered, but decided not to purchase, please share the main reasons why each tool was not chosen.

SOC 2 documentation, EEOC tracking at the level we need, integration with Handshake for our campus operation, those things were either missing or required workarounds. And because recruiting is only part of our HR technology ecosystem, we needed something that played well with our existing HRIS, which Greenhouse's integration with was adequate but not great. SAP SuccessFactors was honestly a disappointment. We had high expectations given SAP's enterprise reputation but the recruiting module felt like an afterthought bolted onto their broader HR suite. The demo was clunky, the interface felt dated even compared to iCIMS, and the sales team was more interested in selling us the entire SAP enterprise package than in addressing our specific recruiting needs. transcript.question: Got it. Now, I'd like to ask you about a few specific recruiting tools. To start, have you heard of BambooHR? If you have, how would you describe it to a colleague? And please share how you feel about this brand? Good or bad.

For that scale, it's perfect. You get a lot of functionality for a reasonable price without the complexity of enterprise systems. I have positive feelings about the brand. It fills an important gap in the market for small businesses that need HR technology but don't have the budget or IT resources for larger platforms.

transcript.question: Have you heard of Workday? If you have, how would you describe it to a colleague? And please share how you feel about this brand? Good or bad.
transcript.response: Workday. I have very strong positive feelings about Workday. If our firm's budget allowed it, we'd be on it tomorrow. The integration across recruiting, talent management, learning, compensation, and workforce planning creates a unified view of your people that no patchwork of point solutions can replicate. I'd describe it to a colleague as the Rolls-Royce of HR technology. You pay a significant premium but you get a product that is genuinely in a different class. transcript.question: Lastly, have you heard of Greenhouse? If you have, how would you describe it to a colleague? And please share how you feel about this brand? Good or bad.
transcript.response: Greenhouse, yes. I was genuinely impressed when we evaluated it. I'd describe it to a colleague as the most thoughtful, well-designed ATS on the market for companies that care about making better hiring decisions. Their philosophy around structured interviewing, reducing unconscious bias, and improving the candidate experience isn't just marketing, it's built into the product at a fundamental level. The scorecard system and the interview planning tools are excellent. I feel very positively about the brand. My only reservation, as I mentioned, is whether it can handle the unique compliance and regulatory requirements of professional services. But for a tech company, a startup, a media company, or really any organization in a less heavily regulated industry, I think Greenhouse is outstanding.

transcript.question: Can you please confirm the main tool that your team uses to recruit new talent?
transcript.response: iCIMS for experienced hire recruiting, and Handshake for campus recruiting. But iCIMS is the primary system of record for overall recruiting operations.

transcript.question: On an annual basis, how much, roughly, do you think your company spends on that tool?
transcript.response: For iCIMS specifically, I think we're paying about 175K a year. transcript.question: Do you think the cost is reasonable relative to the value your company gets?
transcript.response: It's reasonable, with a caveat. For what iCIMS does on the compliance and regulatory documentation side, which is genuinely critical for us, the value is there. SOC 2 audit support, EEOC tracking, regulatory record-keeping, those things are non-negotiable and not every ATS handles them well. But purely on the recruiting functionality front, I don't think we're getting best-in-class value. The sourcing tools are weak, the interview scheduling is adequate at best, and the analytics are behind what platforms like Ashby and Greenhouse offer. So we're paying for compliance infrastructure wrapped in a decent but not exceptional recruiting tool. In our industry, the compliance piece justifies the cost. In a less regulated industry, I'd probably be on a different platform.

transcript.question: Now, please think back to the biggest frustration with your current tool that you shared earlier. Imagine that a feature could be added to your current solution that would solve that frustration. How much do you think that would be worth to your company on an annual basis?
transcript.response: If we could compress the experienced hire interview process and eliminate the scheduling delays that cause us to lose candidates? I think that's worth at least 100K to 150K a year, and I can walk you through the math. We lose approximately 20 to 25 experienced hire candidates per year because our process is too slow. Those are people who made it through multiple interview rounds, who we wanted to hire and who wanted to join us, but who accepted another offer before we could close. If even half of those candidates are senior-level hires, and a productive senior manager or director generates 300K to 500K in annual billing, the revenue impact of losing them is measured in millions. The WTP for a feature that solves this, something like AI-powered scheduling that finds interview slots across multiple busy calendars, or an asynchronous video interview option that eliminates scheduling altogether for early rounds, 100K to 150K is honestly conservative. It would pay for itself within the first quarter.

transcript.question: Lastly, looking at your business at a broader level, what would you say are the biggest challenges affecting your business that are also directly affecting your team?
transcript.response: Talent competition is the number one challenge and it manifests in multiple ways. The Big Four firms have a gravitational pull on the best accounting graduates. They can offer higher starting salaries, more prestigious brand names, and global mobility opportunities that regional firms like ours can't match. We counter with better work-life balance, faster advancement, more client exposure, and a stronger sense of community, and that works for some candidates, but we're always swimming against the tide of Big Four magnetism. The second major challenge is the evolution of our profession. Clients increasingly want advisory services, not just audit and tax compliance. That means we need to recruit people with skills in data analytics, management consulting, technology implementation, cybersecurity, and forensic accounting, people who wouldn't traditionally have considered an accounting firm as an employer. Our recruiting channels and our employer brand aren't fully set up to reach and attract those candidates yet. Third, the remote work question is complicated for us. Client work in audit and tax often requires on-site presence, especially during busy season. But candidates increasingly expect flexibility and remote options. Balancing client service requirements with employee expectations is an ongoing tension that directly affects our ability to attract and retain talent. And finally, the CPA pipeline itself is shrinking. Fewer students are majoring in accounting nationally, and the 150-credit-hour requirement to sit for the CPA exam discourages some students who don't want to invest in a fifth year of college. That's a long-term structural challenge that affects every accounting firm in the country.

transcript.question: Now I'd like to talk about a specific situation. When you or your team needs to recruit new talent, how do you typically handle that today? What software or tools do you use?
transcript.response: So this is a really involved process for us because healthcare recruiting is, I mean, it's a beast. Our primary ATS is Lever. We moved to Lever about two years ago from a legacy system that was, honestly, terrible. So Lever is our core platform. But then we've got a whole ecosystem around it. We use LinkedIn Recruiter for sourcing, especially for leadership and specialty physician roles. We use Indeed for a lot of our clinical support positions, like CNAs, medical assistants, phlebotomists, that kind of thing. We have relationships with about six different staffing agencies that we use for temporary nursing staff. And then for physicians specifically, we work with some physician recruitment firms that specialize in that. We also use a tool called HealthcareSource for some competency assessments, though I'm, I don't know, I'm not a hundred percent sure we're getting full value out of that one. And then we do a lot of job fairs, nursing school partnerships, you know, community outreach. We have a whole team devoted to what we call talent pipeline development, which is basically building relationships with nursing programs and allied health programs at local colleges. It's a lot of moving parts.

transcript.question: Thanks. When you try to recruit new talent, what does a really good outcome look like for you? Why is this important to you or your team?
transcript.response: Oh, great question. A really good outcome, for me, has several components. First, time to fill. We want to get positions filled quickly because in healthcare, an unfilled position doesn't just mean lost productivity, it means patient care is affected. If we're short a nurse on a floor, that means the other nurses have higher patient ratios, which affects quality of care, burnout, everything. So speed matters enormously. Second, quality of hire. We need people who are properly credentialed, clinically competent, and culturally aligned with our patient-first values. I've seen situations where we hired fast but hired the wrong person, and six months later they're gone and we're starting over. Third, and this one is really personal to me, the candidate experience. Healthcare workers talk to each other, especially nurses. If a nurse has a bad experience applying or interviewing with us, they tell their nurse friends, and suddenly we've got a reputation problem in the local nursing community. So a great outcome is filling the role in under 45 days with someone who's going to be a strong performer and who tells their colleagues that we treated them well during the process. That's the trifecta.

transcript.question: Got it. How would you describe your level of satisfaction with how you're currently recruiting new talent? What's working well and what's not?
transcript.response: I'd put us at maybe a six and a half. Which is actually a big improvement from where we were two years ago before we switched to Lever. What's working well is that Lever gives us a much better handle on our pipeline. We can see where candidates are in the process, our recruiters actually like using it, and the interview scheduling integrations save us a lot of back and forth. The partnership work with nursing schools is also paying off, we're starting to see new grads come to us first because of those relationships. What's not working, and this is a significant gap, is the onboarding and credentialing handoff. So a candidate gets through the hiring process in Lever, they accept the offer, and then there's this, like, black hole between offer acceptance and day one. The credentialing, the background checks, the license verification, the drug screening, the occupational health clearance, all of that happens in a different system and sometimes in spreadsheets. And the communication to the candidate during that period is, honestly, not great. We've actually had people accept our offer and then rescind because they got frustrated waiting or didn't hear from us for two weeks while credentialing was being processed. That kills me.

transcript.question: With your current approach, what causes the biggest frustration? Please describe it and the level of frustration it causes you or your team.
transcript.response: The onboarding gap I just described is absolutely the biggest frustration. Let me paint the picture for you. A recruiter works hard for three or four weeks to source a candidate, screen them, coordinate interviews, get the offer approved, get the offer accepted. They're thrilled. And then the candidate enters this credentialing limbo where they're waiting for background check results, waiting for license verification, waiting for references to be called back, waiting for their occupational health appointment. And during that time, the recruiter has basically lost visibility because it's being handled by a different team in a different system. The candidate is calling the recruiter saying, hey, I haven't heard anything, when do I start? And the recruiter has to go chase down the credentialing team for updates. It's messy. I'd put the frustration at a nine out of ten, honestly. We've lost, I think, eight or nine candidates in the past year specifically because the onboarding process took too long or communication broke down during that period. And every one of those lost hires represents probably $8,000 to $10,000 in sunk recruiting costs plus the ongoing cost of the vacancy. transcript.question: To start, please tell me your current seniority and function. As an example, you might say something like: "I'm a senior manager in finance."
transcript.response: Sure, absolutely. I'm the Vice President of Human Resources for a hospitality company. transcript.question: Thanks. I'd like to learn about the company you work for. Which state is the headquarters in? What industry is your company in? And, roughly, how many people work at your company?
transcript.response: We're headquartered in California, in the Bay Area specifically. We operate boutique hotels and resorts along the West Coast, so it's hospitality through and through. In terms of size, we have about 1,200 employees total, though that number fluctuates quite a bit with the seasons. During peak season, like summer and the holidays, we'll bring on an additional 300 to 400 seasonal staff across all our properties. So it's a pretty dynamic workforce situation.

transcript.question: Now I'd like to talk about a specific situation. When you or your team needs to recruit new talent, how do you typically handle that today? What software or tools do you use?
transcript.response: Yeah, so recruiting for us is, I would say, a constant activity rather than something that happens in bursts, although there are definitely peaks. We use Lever as our primary ATS and that handles most of the applicant tracking and pipeline management. On top of that we use Indeed quite heavily because that's where a lot of our hourly candidates are looking. LinkedIn for management and corporate roles. And then for seasonal hiring specifically, we have relationships with hospitality staffing agencies and we do a lot of local outreach, like job fairs at community colleges, partnerships with culinary schools, that sort of thing. It's very much a multi-channel approach because the types of roles we fill are so different. You know, hiring a front desk associate is a completely different process than hiring a director of food and beverage. So the tools we use depend a lot on the role level.

transcript.question: Thanks. When you try to recruit new talent, what does a really good outcome look like for you? Why is this important to you or your team?
transcript.response: Oh, that's a great question. A really good outcome for us, and I think about this a lot honestly, is when we bring someone in who not only has the skills but truly embodies the hospitality mindset. You can train someone to use a POS system or to follow a cleaning checklist, but you can't really train warmth and genuine service orientation. So a great hire for us is someone who makes guests feel taken care of and who meshes with the property's culture. And why is that important? Because in hospitality, your people ARE the product. A guest doesn't remember the thread count of the sheets, but they absolutely remember the person at the front desk who helped them find a last-minute dinner reservation or the housekeeper who left a little note. So when we get hiring right, it directly impacts guest satisfaction scores, online reviews, repeat bookings. When we get it wrong, and I've seen this happen, one disengaged employee can tank a property's TripAdvisor rating. So the stakes are actually really high even though some people think of hospitality hiring as just filling hourly roles.

transcript.question: Got it. How would you describe your level of satisfaction with how you're currently recruiting new talent? What's working well and what's not?
transcript.response: I'd say I'm moderately satisfied, maybe a six out of ten on a good day. What's working well is that Lever gives us decent visibility into where candidates are in the pipeline. The integration with Indeed saves us some time on postings. Our recruiter team is small but scrappy and they know hospitality, so the quality of hires when we do close someone tends to be solid. What's not working is the volume challenge, especially for seasonal hiring. We get absolutely buried in applications in the spring when we're staffing up for summer. I'm talking hundreds and hundreds of applications for entry-level positions, and our screening process is still very manual. My team is spending hours just doing initial phone screens for people who, you know, sometimes don't even show up for the first shift. The other thing that's not working well is that Lever wasn't really built with hospitality in mind. The workflows are designed for, like, tech company hiring where you have structured interview loops. Our process is much faster and more informal for most roles, and the tool doesn't always accommodate that well.

transcript.question: With your current approach, what causes the biggest frustration? Please describe it and the level of frustration it causes you or your team.
transcript.response: The biggest frustration, and this is something I hear from my team constantly, is the no-show problem. We will screen candidates, schedule interviews, sometimes even make offers, and people just vanish. In hospitality, especially for hourly positions, candidates are often applying to ten or fifteen places at once. Whoever calls them back first or offers the most convenient schedule wins. And because our process through Lever has a few steps, even though we've tried to streamline it, we're often not the fastest. My recruiting coordinator literally tracks no-show rates and last quarter it was something like 35 percent for initial interviews at some properties. That is incredibly frustrating for the property managers who block off time to interview and for my team who put the effort into scheduling everything. I'd say it's probably a nine out of ten frustration. It's demoralizing honestly. You feel like you're spinning your wheels.

transcript.question: Now, I'd like you to think back to the last time your team considered buying a new recruiting tool. How long ago was that?
transcript.response: Let me think. That was about eighteen months ago, so late 2024. We went through a pretty thorough evaluation actually. My COO was pushing for us to get more efficient on the hiring side because labor costs were becoming a bigger concern for the board, and she felt like better technology might help us move faster and reduce some of the overhead.

transcript.question: What recruiting tool were you using at the time and which recruiting tools did you consider buying?
transcript.response: We were using Lever, same as now. And we evaluated, let me recall, we looked at Jobvite, we looked at iCIMS, and we also took a demo of Greenhouse. So three alternatives total. I wanted to look at tools that had high-volume hiring capabilities because that's really where our pain was.

transcript.question: Was a contract for your existing tool expiring? And were you happy or frustrated with your existing tool?
transcript.response: The Lever contract wasn't expiring for another six months at that point, but we wanted to get ahead of it and have a decision made before renewal time. And to your second question, I'd say we were increasingly frustrated. Not with everything, Lever does some things well, but the high-volume hiring piece was just not cutting it. We felt like we were using a tool designed for a different kind of company and trying to force it to work for hospitality. Which, to be fair to Lever, it is designed for a different kind of company. So it wasn't really their fault, but it was still frustrating for us.

transcript.question: Were there any changes in your business that motivated your team to consider buying a new recruiting tool? Did your recruiting needs change?
transcript.response: Yes, definitely. We had opened two new properties in the previous year, which added about 250 positions that needed to be filled. And we were planning to open another one in 2025. So our hiring volume was going up significantly while our HR team stayed the same size. On top of that, we were seeing more turnover industry-wide after the pandemic, which meant we were not just filling new roles but constantly backfilling existing ones. So the needs absolutely changed in terms of scale, and our existing tools weren't scaling with us.

transcript.question: Which recruiting tools did you consider? Please list the names of the tools you considered.
transcript.response: Jobvite, iCIMS, and Greenhouse. Those were the three we formally evaluated with demos and pricing.

transcript.question: After looking at those tools, did you purchase one or just continue using your current tool?
transcript.response: We ended up purchasing iCIMS, actually. We're in the process of migrating right now. Well, I should say we just finished the core migration and we're in the adoption phase where teams are still getting used to it.

transcript.question: If you purchased one, which one did you purchase and what attracted you to it? How did it stand out from the others you considered?
transcript.response: We went with iCIMS. What attracted us most was their high-volume hiring capabilities. They have features specifically designed for companies that need to process hundreds of applications quickly, like automated screening questions, text-based recruiting which is huge for hourly workers who don't check email, and really strong career site tools. They also had good case studies from other hospitality and retail companies which gave me confidence that they understood our world. What really made it stand out was the text recruiting feature. When I saw that candidates could apply and be screened via text message, I immediately thought about our no-show problem. If we can engage candidates in the channel they actually use and move faster, we should be able to reduce those drop-offs. That was the clincher for me.

transcript.question: For each of the tools that you considered, but decided not to purchase, please share the main reasons why each tool was not chosen.
transcript.response: Sure. Jobvite was, you know, decent but it felt like it was kind of in between. Not as robust as iCIMS for high-volume but more than we needed in some other areas. The pricing was also not that different from iCIMS so it was hard to justify choosing the less capable option at a similar price point. Greenhouse I have a lot of respect for, but it's really built for tech company hiring with structured interview processes and scorecards and all of that. Which is great if you're hiring software engineers, but for hiring housekeepers and line cooks, it was way more process than we needed and the pricing reflected that level of sophistication. It felt like we'd be paying for features we'd never use.

transcript.question: Got it. Now, I'd like to ask you about a few specific recruiting tools. To start, have you heard of BambooHR? If you have, how would you describe it to a colleague? And please share how you feel about this brand? Good or bad.
transcript.response: Oh yes, I know BambooHR. We actually used it at a previous company I was at, a much smaller boutique hotel group. I'd describe it as a really user-friendly HR platform that's great for small businesses. The interface is clean, the onboarding module is nice, and it covers the basics really well. For recruiting though, it's pretty limited. You can post jobs and track applicants but it doesn't have the depth you need once you're past maybe a hundred employees doing regular hiring. My feeling about the brand is generally positive. I think they serve their target market well. They're just not built for companies that have outgrown the small business phase.

transcript.question: Have you heard of Workday? If you have, how would you describe it to a colleague? And please share how you feel about this brand? Good or bad.
transcript.response: Absolutely, Workday is kind of the gold standard for large enterprise HR and finance. I have a few colleagues at big hotel chains like Marriott and Hilton who use Workday and they, you know, it's a love-hate relationship from what I hear. Incredibly powerful, incredibly comprehensive, but also incredibly complex and expensive to implement. For a company our size it's not even in the conversation. My feelings are that it's a strong brand with a great product for the right customer. But I've heard the implementation process can take over a year and cost more than the software itself, so that's always given me pause.

transcript.question: Lastly, have you heard of Greenhouse? If you have, how would you describe it to a colleague? And please share how you feel about this brand? Good or bad.
transcript.response: Yes, we looked at Greenhouse during our evaluation like I mentioned. I'd describe it to a colleague as probably the best ATS for companies that want very structured, data-driven hiring processes. Their scorecards and interview kits are really well designed. I have positive feelings about the brand overall. The product is polished and the company seems to genuinely care about reducing bias in hiring, which I appreciate. It just wasn't the right fit for our specific use case in hospitality where speed matters more than process rigor for most of our positions.

transcript.question: Can you please confirm the main tool that your team uses to recruit new talent?
transcript.response: Well, technically we're transitioning. We're moving from Lever to iCIMS. But I'd say right now we're primarily using Lever still while iCIMS is being rolled out across properties.

transcript.question: On an annual basis, how much, roughly, do you think your company spends on that tool?
transcript.response: On Lever we were paying about 90K a year. The iCIMS contract is higher, it's around 140K annually, but that includes the text recruiting module and some additional features we didn't have before. So it's a significant step up in cost but we believe the ROI will be there.

transcript.question: Do you think the cost is reasonable relative to the value your company gets?
transcript.response: For Lever at 90K, I'd say it was borderline. We were paying a lot for a tool that wasn't fully meeting our needs. For iCIMS at 140K, I think it will be reasonable once we're fully adopted. The text recruiting alone should save us significant time and improve our candidate engagement. Ask me again in six months and I'll have a better answer on whether the value is truly there.

transcript.question: Now, please think back to the biggest frustration with your current tool that you shared earlier. Imagine that a feature could be added to your current solution that would solve that frustration. How much do you think that would be worth to your company on an annual basis?
transcript.response: The no-show problem, right. So if a feature could genuinely solve that, and I mean really solve it, like cut our no-show rate from 35 percent to under 10 percent? That would be enormous. I've done the math on this actually. Each no-show costs us maybe two to three hours of recruiter and manager time. Multiply that by the volume we do, and it adds up fast. I'd estimate it would be worth 50 to 75K a year to us, easily. Maybe more when you factor in the faster time to fill and reduced overtime costs from being short-staffed. That's actually one of the reasons we bought iCIMS, because the text recruiting feature should help address this.

transcript.question: Lastly, looking at your business at a broader level, what would you say are the biggest challenges affecting your business that are also directly affecting your team?
transcript.response: Oh, there are a few big ones. First, labor costs in hospitality are rising faster than room rates, which squeezes margins and makes my CFO very nervous about headcount. Second, the whole industry is still dealing with a workforce perception problem from the pandemic. A lot of people left hospitality and went to other industries and haven't come back. The labor pool is smaller than it used to be, especially for experienced roles like sous chefs or experienced front office managers. Third, and this is more California-specific, the regulatory environment keeps getting more complex. New labor laws, minimum wage increases, scheduling regulations. All of that adds compliance burden to my team and makes it harder to be nimble with hiring. And lastly, guest expectations keep rising because of all these boutique hotel brands and Airbnb raising the bar on personalized experience. Which means we need better talent, not just more talent, and that's a harder recruiting challenge to solve with technology alone.

transcript.question: To start, please tell me your current seniority and function. As an example, you might say something like: "I'm a senior manager in finance."
transcript.response: Sure. I'm a manager of talent acquisition for a healthcare system. So I run a team of recruiters who focus specifically on clinical hiring, which is nurses, medical assistants, therapists, that kind of thing. I also support some of the non-clinical hiring but the clinical side takes up probably 80 percent of my time because that's where the volume and urgency is.

transcript.question: Thanks. I'd like to learn about the company you work for. Which state is the headquarters in? What industry is your company in? And, roughly, how many people work at your company?
transcript.response: We're headquartered in New Jersey. We're a regional healthcare system, so we operate hospitals, outpatient clinics, urgent care centers, and some specialty practices. In terms of employees, we have about 5,500 people across all of our locations. It's a big operation. We're one of the larger employers in our part of the state actually, which has its own pros and cons when it comes to recruiting because everybody knows who we are, which is good, but we're also competing with two other health systems in the same area for the same nurses.

transcript.question: Now I'd like to talk about a specific situation. When you or your team needs to recruit new talent, how do you typically handle that today? What software or tools do you use?
transcript.response: Okay, so our primary system is iCIMS. That's our ATS and it's where everything lives, the job postings, applications, interview scheduling, offer letters, all of it. On top of that we use LinkedIn Recruiter for sourcing, especially for hard-to-fill positions like specialized nurses or clinical leadership roles. We also post heavily on Indeed and we use some healthcare-specific job boards like Health eCareers and NurseFly. For travel nurse positions, which we unfortunately rely on more than I'd like, we work with several staffing agencies. And then honestly there's still a lot of, you know, grassroots recruiting. We do career fairs at nursing schools, we have an employee referral program that generates maybe 20 percent of our hires, and our recruiters do a lot of direct outreach on LinkedIn. So it's a whole ecosystem of tools and channels, and iCIMS is sort of the hub that ties it all together.

transcript.question: Thanks. When you try to recruit new talent, what does a really good outcome look like for you? Why is this important to you or your team?
transcript.response: A really good outcome, and I mean like the ideal scenario, is when we find a qualified clinician, let's say an RN with the right specialty certification, and we get them from application to accepted offer within three weeks. And then they show up for orientation and they're still there six months later. That's the dream scenario. Why is it important? Oh my gosh, where do I start. Every day that a nursing position is open, we're either paying for a travel nurse at two or three times the cost, or we're asking our existing nurses to work overtime, which leads to burnout, which leads to more turnover, which creates more open positions. It's a vicious cycle. I've seen the data on what one open nursing position costs the organization per week and it's staggering. We're talking thousands of dollars in agency fees, overtime, and lost productivity. So when we get a hire right and fast, it literally saves the organization money and keeps our existing staff from burning out. The clinical quality piece matters too, obviously. You want nurses who are competent and caring because patient outcomes depend on it.

transcript.question: Got it. How would you describe your level of satisfaction with how you're currently recruiting new talent? What's working well and what's not?
transcript.response: I would say I'm about a five out of ten satisfied, which is not great. What's working well, honestly, is the people on my team. They are incredibly dedicated and they hustle. The employee referral program is also working well, we get good quality candidates through referrals and they tend to stay longer. iCIMS is working okay as a system of record, like it does the job of tracking applicants and managing the workflow. What's not working is the speed. Healthcare recruiting has gotten so competitive that by the time we get through our process, which involves credentialing verification, background checks, reference checks, and sometimes licensure verification, the candidate has already accepted an offer somewhere else. The other health system down the road might have a faster process or they might offer a bigger sign-on bonus, and we lose the candidate. The other thing that's not working well is our career site experience. It's powered by iCIMS and it's, I mean, it's functional but it's not going to win any awards. Nurses applying on their phones find it clunky, and we know we lose people at the application stage because of that.

transcript.question: With your current approach, what causes the biggest frustration? Please describe it and the level of frustration it causes you or your team.
transcript.response: The biggest frustration, and this is something that keeps me up at night honestly, is losing candidates to competitors at the offer stage. We'll invest all this time sourcing, screening, interviewing, checking credentials, and then when we're ready to make the offer, the candidate says they already accepted somewhere else. Or sometimes even worse, they accept our offer and then ghost us before their start date because they got a better sign-on bonus from another hospital. It's devastating for my team. A recruiter might spend 15 to 20 hours on a single nursing candidate, building the relationship, coordinating interviews with the nurse manager, pushing the credentialing through. And then it all evaporates. I would put the frustration level at a solid nine. It's really demoralizing and it makes it hard to feel like you're making progress. My recruiters are doing the work but the market is so tight that a lot of that work doesn't result in hires. And that impacts their morale, which then impacts their productivity, which is another cycle I have to manage.

And then there's the generational shift, a lot of senior advisors are retiring and we need to backfill with younger talent who often need more training.

transcript.question: To start, please tell me your current seniority and function. As an example, you might say something like: "I'm a senior manager in finance."
transcript.response: Sure. I'm a director of people operations, so basically I oversee all of HR but with a heavy focus on talent acquisition because at our stage, hiring is everything. I report directly to our CEO.

transcript.question: Thanks. I'd like to learn about the company you work for. Which state is the headquarters in? What industry is your company in? And, roughly, how many people work at your company?
transcript.response: We're based in Portland, Oregon. We're a B2B SaaS company, we build supply chain optimization software for mid-market manufacturers. Currently about 180 employees. When I joined two years ago we were at 90, so we've basically doubled. And the plan is to get to about 300 by end of next year if our Series C funding comes through, which, fingers crossed, should happen in Q3. So we're in this really intense growth phase where every hire matters because each person represents a meaningful percentage of the company.

transcript.question: Now I'd like to talk about a specific situation. When you or your team needs to recruit new talent, how do you typically handle that today? What software or tools do you use?
transcript.response: So our primary ATS is Lever. We've been on Lever since before I joined and honestly it's worked pretty well for us through this growth phase. For sourcing, we lean heavily on LinkedIn Recruiter. For engineering roles specifically, which are probably 40% of our open positions at any given time, we also use Wellfound, which used to be AngelList Talent. And we've started experimenting with a tool called Gem for candidate outreach sequencing because our response rates were dropping when we were just doing manual LinkedIn InMails. We have two full-time recruiters plus me. One recruiter focuses on engineering and product, the other handles go-to-market and G&A roles. I step in for director-level and above. We also use HackerRank for technical assessments and Calendly for scheduling, though we're thinking about switching to a more integrated scheduling solution. Oh, and for reference checks we use Crosschq. So yeah, the stack is bigger than you'd think for a company our size, but each tool serves a purpose.

transcript.question: Thanks. When you try to recruit new talent, what does a really good outcome look like for you? Why is this important to you or your team?
transcript.response: Great question. A really good outcome, and I think about this a lot, has three dimensions. First, speed. We're competing with every other funded startup in Portland and the broader remote market for engineering talent. If we can't move fast, we lose candidates to companies like Zapier or GitLab or whoever else is recruiting remotely. So a fast process, ideally from first contact to offer in three weeks or less, is critical. Second, quality. At our size, one bad engineering hire can set a team back months. We need people who are not just technically strong but who can thrive in a startup environment where requirements shift, where you might be the only person working on a feature, where you need to figure things out without a lot of hand-holding. Third, and this one is underappreciated, candidate experience. We're building a brand as an employer and every candidate interaction reflects on us. Even people we don't hire talk about their experience, especially in Portland's tech community which is smaller than you'd think. So a good outcome is someone who joins, ramps up quickly, ships meaningful work within the first quarter, and tells their friends it was a great interview process. That last part is important because referrals are our highest-converting source.

transcript.question: Got it. How would you describe your level of satisfaction with how you're currently recruiting new talent? What's working well and what's not?
transcript.response: I'd give us a six, maybe a six and a half. What's working well is the process itself. We've built a pretty disciplined hiring workflow in Lever with structured scorecards, debrief templates, and clear stage gates. The interviewers generally know what they're evaluating and we've reduced the number of 'gut feel' hires significantly since I implemented that. Lever's candidate tagging and pipeline management is good. LinkedIn Recruiter is expensive but effective for sourcing. Our referral program generates about 25% of our hires which is strong. What's not working is scale. The tools work fine when we're hiring 5 to 8 people a quarter, but we're now trying to hire 15 to 20 per quarter and the manual parts of the process are becoming bottlenecks. Things like scheduling, sending personalized outreach at volume, and consolidating feedback from interview panels. My recruiters are spending too much time on administrative coordination and not enough on actual relationship-building with candidates. Also, the data across our tools is fragmented. Lever has our pipeline data, Gem has outreach metrics, LinkedIn has source data, and HackerRank has assessment scores. Getting a unified view of our recruiting funnel performance requires manual spreadsheet work, and we just don't have time for that.

transcript.question: With your current approach, what causes the biggest frustration? Please describe it and the level of frustration it causes you or your team.
transcript.response: The biggest frustration is the time my recruiters spend on scheduling and coordination rather than actually sourcing and building candidate relationships. We did a time study last quarter and found that each recruiter was spending about 30% of their week on scheduling logistics, following up with interviewers for feedback, chasing down scorecards, and managing the back-and-forth of panel coordination. That's a day and a half per week per recruiter that's not going toward finding great candidates. And the frustrating part is it's entirely solvable with better tooling and automation, but Lever's scheduling capabilities are basic and we haven't found an integration that works seamlessly. We tried Calendly but it doesn't handle panel interviews well. We looked at GoodTime but the pricing was steep for our size. So we're stuck in this manual mode and it's frustrating because we know it's inefficient. I'd rate the frustration at an eight out of ten. It's the kind of thing that doesn't feel urgent on any given day but cumulatively it's costing us maybe one additional hire per quarter that we're missing because our recruiters don't have enough sourcing hours.

transcript.question: Now, I'd like you to think back to the last time your team considered buying a new recruiting tool. How long ago was that?
transcript.response: About six months ago. We spent maybe three or four weeks looking at options. It coincided with our annual planning cycle so there was actually budget available, which doesn't always happen at a startup.

transcript.question: What recruiting tool were you using at the time and which recruiting tools did you consider buying?
transcript.response: We were and still are on Lever. We looked at switching to Greenhouse, and we also looked at Ashby, which is a newer ATS that's gotten a lot of buzz in the startup community. And we evaluated whether to keep Lever and add Gem as a more integrated CRM layer.

transcript.question: Was a contract for your existing tool expiring? And were you happy or frustrated with your existing tool?
transcript.response: The contract wasn't expiring, we had about eight months left. But we could have negotiated an early switch if we wanted to. I'd say we were, I don't know, moderately satisfied but aware of its limitations. Lever is a good tool but it hasn't evolved as much as some of the newer platforms. It feels like the product development has slowed down. The core ATS functionality is solid but the ancillary stuff, analytics, automation, scheduling, feel a generation behind what some competitors are offering. So it wasn't frustration so much as awareness that we could be doing better.

transcript.question: Were there any changes in your business that motivated your team to consider buying a new recruiting tool? Did your recruiting needs change?
transcript.response: Yes, several things. The biggest was the Series C planning. Our board approved a hiring plan that would roughly double the company over 18 months. That forced us to ask, can our current tools handle double the volume? And the honest answer was, not without adding a third recruiter, which we'd rather avoid if better automation could close the gap. We also started hiring more remote roles which added complexity around scheduling across time zones. And frankly, seeing peers at other Portland startups talk about their experience with Ashby and Greenhouse made us curious about whether we were missing out on better tooling.

transcript.question: Which recruiting tools did you consider? Please list the names of the tools you considered.
transcript.response: Greenhouse, Ashby, and the option of adding Gem on top of Lever.

transcript.question: After looking at those tools, did you purchase one or just continue using your current tool?
transcript.response: We ended up adding Gem on top of Lever rather than switching ATS platforms. So we didn't replace Lever but we did purchase Gem.

transcript.question: If you purchased one, which one did you purchase and what attracted you to it? How did it stand out from the others you considered?
transcript.response: We purchased Gem. What attracted us was that it solved our biggest pain point, outreach and engagement, without requiring a full ATS migration. The automated sequencing for candidate outreach was immediately valuable. We could set up multi-touch email and LinkedIn sequences and track response rates in a way we couldn't before. The analytics were also a draw. Gem gives us a clear view of our pipeline velocity and source effectiveness that we were cobbling together manually before. It integrates with Lever well enough that we didn't have to rip and replace our whole workflow. And the pricing was reasonable for a company our size. Compared to switching to Greenhouse or Ashby, which would have meant weeks of migration, retraining, and rebuilding our interview workflows, Gem was the path of least disruption with the highest near-term impact.

transcript.question: For each of the tools that you considered, but decided not to purchase, please share the main reasons why each tool was not chosen.
transcript.response: Greenhouse was the strongest overall platform of the three we looked at. The structured hiring methodology is really well thought out and the analytics are excellent. But the migration cost and effort was the dealbreaker. We estimated it would take six to eight weeks to fully transition, and during that time our hiring would slow down at exactly the moment we needed to accelerate. The other concern was price. Greenhouse was going to cost us about 40% more than Lever on an annual basis, which is meaningful at our stage. Ashby was really interesting and honestly it was tempting. The UI is beautiful, the built-in scheduling is exactly what we need, and the all-in-one approach means fewer tools to manage. But it's a younger company and the platform is still maturing in some areas. A few people I talked to who used it said they hit edge cases where features they expected didn't exist yet. At our growth stage, I couldn't risk adopting a platform that might have gaps we'd discover at the worst possible time. I want to revisit Ashby in a year or so when it's more mature.

transcript.question: Got it. Now, I'd like to ask you about a few specific recruiting tools. To start, have you heard of BambooHR? If you have, how would you describe it to a colleague? And please share how you feel about this brand? Good or bad.
transcript.response: Yeah, I've heard of BambooHR. I'd describe it to a colleague as an all-in-one HR platform that's designed for small businesses. It handles things like employee records, PTO tracking, onboarding, benefits administration, and it has a recruiting module, but the recruiting piece is pretty basic. It's essentially an HR information system with an ATS bolted on. My feeling is that it's a perfectly fine product for companies in that like, 20 to 150 employee range where you need one person in HR to manage everything and you want it all in one place. When we were at 50 employees before my time, we were actually on BambooHR and it worked. But once you start hiring seriously, more than a few people a month, you outgrow the recruiting functionality fast. The candidate pipeline management is limited, the reporting is surface level, and you can't really customize interview workflows the way you can in a dedicated ATS. So positive feeling for what it is, but it's not a serious recruiting tool for a company in growth mode.

transcript.question: Have you heard of Workday? If you have, how would you describe it to a colleague? And please share how you feel about this brand? Good or bad.
transcript.response: I've heard of Workday for sure but it's not really in our universe. I'd describe it as the big enterprise HR and finance platform that large companies use. Think Fortune 500 type stuff. It does everything from HR to payroll to financial planning. My feeling is that it's a powerful system for companies that need it but it would be absurd for us. The implementation cost alone would probably be more than our entire annual HR budget. I've talked to HR leaders at large companies who use it and the consensus seems to be that it's comprehensive but complex and the recruiting module specifically isn't its strongest suit. Most Workday customers I know still pair it with a dedicated ATS. So my feeling is respectful but it's like, you know, describing a Ferrari to someone who drives a Honda. It's great for the right buyer but that's not us.

transcript.question: Lastly, have you heard of Greenhouse? If you have, how would you describe it to a colleague? And please share how you feel about this brand? Good or bad.
transcript.response: Yes, we just evaluated Greenhouse seriously. I'd describe it as probably the gold standard ATS for tech companies and knowledge-worker hiring. They've built the product around this philosophy of structured hiring, where every interview has a defined purpose, every interviewer uses scorecards, and hiring decisions are driven by data rather than gut feel. The analytics are really strong and the integrations ecosystem is robust. My feeling is very positive on the product. If we were starting fresh today, I'd probably choose Greenhouse over Lever. The reason we didn't switch is purely practical, migration cost and timing. But I think Greenhouse has done an excellent job of defining what modern recruiting should look like. I recommend it to peers when they ask.

transcript.question: Can you please confirm the main tool that your team uses to recruit new talent?
transcript.response: Lever is our primary ATS, now supplemented by Gem for sourcing and outreach.

transcript.question: On an annual basis, how much, roughly, do you think your company spends on that tool?
transcript.response: So for the full recruiting tech stack, Lever is about 28,000 a year, Gem is another 18,000, LinkedIn Recruiter is about 22,000. So we're looking at roughly 68,000 total across the primary tools. Plus HackerRank and some smaller things, it's probably close to 80,000 all in. For just Lever itself, about 28,000.

transcript.question: Do you think the cost is reasonable relative to the value your company gets?
transcript.response: For Lever specifically, yes, it's reasonable. 28K for a solid ATS at our volume is fair. The overall 80K spend on the full stack gives me some pause just because it's a lot of point solutions and I wonder if a more integrated platform could deliver the same value for less. But each tool earns its keep individually. The cost per hire when you factor in the tech stack is probably around 1,000 to 1,200 which is decent for software engineering hires in this market.

transcript.question: Now, please think back to the biggest frustration with your current tool that you shared earlier. Imagine that a feature could be added to your current solution that would solve that frustration. How much do you think that would be worth to your company on an annual basis?
transcript.response: If we could get back that 30% of recruiter time that's going to scheduling and coordination, let me think about this. Each recruiter costs us about 90,000 fully loaded. Thirty percent of that is 27,000 per recruiter, times two recruiters, that's 54,000 in recovered productivity. But the real value isn't just the cost savings, it's the additional hires those hours would generate. If each recruiter could source and close even two more hires per quarter because they had more time for relationship-building, at an average employee value of whatever, I'd say the feature would be worth 50,000 to 75,000 a year to us. And that's probably conservative.

transcript.question: Lastly, looking at your business at a broader level, what would you say are the biggest challenges affecting your business that are also directly affecting your team?
transcript.response: The big one is the competition for engineering talent. Every SaaS company, every startup, every big tech company is hiring software engineers and the supply just isn't keeping up with demand. Remote work has made it worse in some ways because now we're not just competing with Portland companies, we're competing with everyone. A candidate we're talking to might also be interviewing at Stripe, Notion, and a dozen other companies. So we have to move fast and sell the opportunity hard. The second challenge is capital efficiency pressure. Our investors want us to grow but also demonstrate a path to profitability. That tension directly affects my team because there's pressure to hire more people but also pressure to keep headcount costs down. We have to be very strategic about which roles we fill versus which ones we try to cover with existing people or contractors. And the third thing is just the broader economic uncertainty. We sell to manufacturers and if the economy softens, our sales cycle lengthens, which affects revenue projections, which affects the hiring plan. We've already pushed a few roles out by a quarter because of pipeline uncertainty. My team has to be ready to accelerate or decelerate hiring on short notice, which is hard when you're trying to build relationships with candidates.
